records.title: “Tell Me What You Eat”: Literary Perspectives on Food and Culture
records.speaker: Prof. Supriya M. Nair
records.speaker_title: Professor, Department of English Language and Literature
records.description: “One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well," notes the narrator in Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own. Amidst an increasing focus on gut health, sustainable food systems, food sovereignty, food (in)security, and other social (and social media) topics, the place of food in literature and culture has come in for renewed interest in scholarship that goes beyond the gustatory text. How do a range of literary forms (fiction, nonfiction, cookbooks) and visual media help us imagine the significant ways in which food relates to our lived experience? If food has power, as Anthony Bourdain insists in Kitchen Confidential, how does literature reveal its power?
records.speaker_bio: Supriya M. Nair is a Professor in the Department of English Language and Literature at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor. She is the author of two monographs, Caliban’s Curse: George Lamming and the Revisioning of History and Pathologies of Paradise: Caribbean Detours. She is also co-editor of Postcolonialisms: An Anthology of Cultural Theory and Criticism and editor of Teaching Anglophone Caribbean Literature. She regularly teaches courses on Food and Culture at the University of Michigan.
records.notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Diverse Dimensions of Art
records.title: Screenwriting: The Hero’s Journey in 3 Acts
records.speaker: R. J. Fox
records.speaker_title: Writer, filmmaker, and teacher of English and film
records.description: The speaker will demonstrate how just about every movie – from Hollywood blockbuster or to small, indie film – follows the same story structure, divided by three acts and 12 steps along the “the Hero’s Journey.” In addition to providing examples of story structure in popular films, Fox will also touch upon screenplay formatting. There will also be an interactive component in which participants can explore these concepts through their favorite films.
records.speaker_bio: R.J. Fox is the award-winning writer of three published books, several short stories, plays, poems, a memoir, and 15 feature-length screenplays. He is also the writer/director/editor of several award-winning short films. He teaches English and film at Huron High School in Ann Arbor, MI. His movie Love & Vodka (based on his book of the same name) premiered at the 2024 Cinetopia Film festival.
records.notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.

records.title: Conversations
records.description: “CONVERSATIONS” provides OLLI-UM members with a reprieve from digital devices and the outside world, offering opportunities to explore edgy and occasionally controversial topics that broaden our horizons and deepen our understanding. We’ll interview distinguished faculty members who are captivating and sometimes controversial. They are all helping shape the future through their interaction with students, our future leaders. The interview will be one hour long with 30 minutes for audience Q & A.
records.notes: In-person at Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Pond Room. $15 Member | $25 Non-Member.

records.title: Presidential Power Unleashed: Trump, The Unitary Executive, and What Comes Next
records.speaker: Mitchel Sollenberger, Ph.D.
records.speaker_title: Professor of Political Science; Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education and Student Success
records.description: When a President proclaims that he may ‘do whatever he wants,’ one must ask: what becomes of the delicate balance that the Framers sought to establish? Political scientist Mitchel Sollenberger invites us to interrogate the core of American constitutional government by asking whether the doctrine of the unitary executive has shifted from interpretive theory into a partisan instrument of political power. In an era in which the presidency under Donald Trump is redefining the breadth of executive reach, the essential question is no longer simply what powers the President holds, but rather what meaningful powers remain for Congress, the courts, and, ultimately, the citizenry.
records.speaker_bio: Mitchel A. Sollenberger, Ph.D stands out as a scholar-administrator whose intellectual rigor and public spirit illuminate the contours of American constitutional order. As Professor of Political Science at UM-Dearborn and Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education and Student Success, he blends deep academic expertise with institutional leadership. His award-winning research—books like The Unitary Executive Theory: A Danger to Constitutional Government and The President’s Czars—and his prolific writings in top journals show unflinching clarity in confronting how executive power is expanding.
records.notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person only.

records.title: When Good Intentions Go Wrong: Campus Activism vs. Academic Freedom
records.speaker: Jeffrey Veidlinger, Ph.D.
records.speaker_title: Joseph Brodsky Collegiate Professor of History and Judaic Studies; inaugural director, Raoul Wallenberg Institute
records.description: When do the noblest intentions betray the very freedoms they endeavor to safeguard? In this interview, we will probe the tension between zeal and expression, between cause and constraint. Can activism that aspires to justice become a form of silence? Join us in exploring the paradox inherent in protecting vulnerable communities while preserving open scholarly discourse.
records.speaker_bio: Jeffrey Veidlinger, Ph.D., the inaugural director of the Raoul Wallenberg Institute at the University of Michigan, is a distinguished scholar whose work bridges history, culture, and human rights. As the Joseph Brodsky Collegiate Professor of History and Judaic Studies, he has authored acclaimed books such as In the Midst of Civilized Europe, which examines the pogroms of 1918–1921 and their role in the onset of the Holocaust.
records.notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person only.

records.title: Healing the Mind: Must We Accept Cognitive Decline? The Role of Psychedelics (Psilocybin) in Treatments
records.speaker: Omar Ahmed, Ph.D.
records.speaker_title: Associate Professor of Psychology, Neuroscience, and Biomedical Engineering
records.description: What if the path to healing the mind isn’t just about suppressing symptoms, but about rewiring the brain itself? Dr. Omar J. Ahmed’s research challenges conventional wisdom by demonstrating that psychedelics can induce lasting neuroplasticity, even in regions previously thought unaffected. His work invites us to reconsider: Could a single dose of a psychedelic compound be the key to unlocking long-term relief from Alzheimer’s, Dementia, Depression, and possible other cognitive disabilities, reshaping our understanding of mental health treatment?
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Omar J. Ahmed is an Associate Professor at the University of Michigan, specializing in Psychology, Neuroscience, and Biomedical Engineering. His lab, OmarLab, investigates how neural circuits, particularly in the retrosplenial cortex, encode space, time, and speed.
records.notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person only.

records.title: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
records.description: Join us in the search for the nature, meaning and consequences of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections across the nation and in Michigan. Learn about the historical patterns of midterm election results and how 2026 may or may not fit with them. Discover insights into the role consumption of information on social media impacts the perceptions and behaviors of voters in U.S. elections. Assess how the public perceptions of the policies adopted in the previous two years of a presidency impacts election outcomes. In turn, consider how to think about the consequences for Congress and the President in public policymaking after the 2026 midterms. A 2026 Midterm Elections Contest will be held this fall. Further details to follow.
records.notes: 5 weekly lectures. $15/day pass (members), $25/day pass (non-members), $70 for the entire 5-week series. In-person at Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium, and live streamed through Zoom. The Thursday section is branded "Thursday Lectures: Thoughtful Talks for Curious Minds" in this catalog. Planned by Richard Barron, Ron Bogdasarian, Donna Clack, Jeff Gaynor, Larry Imerman, Jerry Newman and chair Craig Ramsay.

records.title: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
records.description: This series invites you to explore a region in rapid transition, where geopolitics, economic opportunity, and environmental challenges converge. Leading experts will examine the history, regional power dynamics, development in North America, Europe and Russia, and the profound local and global impacts of climate change on human, wildlife and plant ecosystems. Together, these perspectives offer a deeper understanding of why the Arctic matters—not only to those who live there, but to the future of the global community.
records.notes: 5 weekly lectures. $15/day pass (members), $25/day pass (non-members), $70 for the entire 5-week series. Four of the five speakers presented live on Zoom (George Kling in person at WCC). Concludes with a ticketed Arctic Buffet Lunch in the Pond Room (Nov 19, 2026, 11:30 am - 1:30 pm, $20 per person). Planned by Larry Imerman, Camille Orso, Anne Preston and co-chairs Frances Schultz and Katherine Woo.

records.title: Conversations
records.description: America at 250: Will the Experiment Last? — In 1787, James Madison confronted a question that still haunts us: Can a republic survive itself? Two hundred and fifty years later, with money flooding politics and democratic institutions straining under pressures the founders both anticipated and feared, that question feels more urgent than ever. America at 250: Will the Experiment Last? is a series of conversations with University of Michigan scholars who have spent their careers examining democracy not as an ideal, but as a living, fragile, and contested experiment. The founders warned us. We’re still deciding whether we listened.
records.notes: First Conversations season with an explicit theme (America at 250: Will the Experiment Last?). Interview format: a one-hour interview with 30 minutes of audience Q&A. In-person only at Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Pond Room. $15 Member | $25 Non-Member.

records.title: Regulating Business in America: A Long-Term Perspective
records.speaker: Prof. William James (Jim) Adams
records.speaker_title: Arthur F. Thurnau Professor Emeritus, Professor Emeritus of Economics, and former Peterson Professor of Industrial Organization
records.description: Since the Civil War, the United States has experienced periodic waves of regulatory and deregulatory fervor. The pro-regulation tendency is associated with the Progressive agendas of the two Roosevelts (Teddy and Franklin), while the anti-regulation tendency is associated with the Supreme Courts of the late-nineteenth and late-twentieth centuries. Drawing on the regulation of business in different types of markets (labor markets, industrial markets, public utilities) and different types of regulatory institution (legislatures, administrative agencies), this lecture will explore the economic and legal ideas, as well as the economic realities, that shaped these turns in American regulatory history.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. William James (Jim) Adams is Arthur F. Thurnau Professor Emeritus, Professor Emeritus of Economics, and the former Peterson Professor of Industrial Organization at the University of Michigan. His research has ranged broadly, from public policies toward business in the United States to economic integration in Europe. His monograph, Restructuring the French Economy: Government and the Rise of Market Competition since World War II, has been called “one of the most penetrating [and] comprehensive analyses of French contemporary economic reality.” Adams has advised the Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. Ambassador to France, and several foreign policy departments of the U.S. government. He is a winner of a Golden Apple, awarded each year by students to the best teacher at the University of Michigan.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person (Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium) and online via Zoom. Sponsorship: Aetna.

records.title: America’s First Medical Experiments in the Wilds of Northern Michigan: A 19th Century Physician’s 33-Year Study of Digestion via a Fur Trader’s Abdominal Shotgun Wound
records.speaker: Prof. Joel D. Howell
records.speaker_title: Elizabeth Farrand Professor Emeritus, Departments of Internal Medicine and History
records.description: In 1822 the fur trader Alexis St. Martin suffered a shotgun wound on Mackinaw Island. He was attended by the physician William Beaumont. The blast left a hole in St. Martin’s abdomen, and for the next 33 years Beaumont did experiments through that opening. We will explore their travels together through the wilderness of the early republic, discuss how the experiments led to our current understanding of gastrointestinal physiology, and question the ethics of how Beaumont chose to experiment on St. Martin.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Joel D. Howell is the Elizabeth Farrand Professor Emeritus in the University of Michigan Departments of Internal Medicine and History. He obtained his MD at the University of Chicago and his PhD in History and Sociology of Science from the University of Pennsylvania. His career has included clinical care and studying medical history, trying to understand why (and when) we came to believe so strongly in the value of science for guiding patient care. Author of many books and articles, Howell’s publications have appeared widely in medical and historical literature. His research has been supported both by federal grants and by foundations. His awards include the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Investigator Award in Health Policy Research and the Burroughs Wellcome Award in the History of Medicine. Prof. Howell is a Master of the American College of Physicians and Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person (Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium) and online via Zoom. Sponsorship: UM Victors Care.

records.title: The U.S. Midterm Elections: What Happened Last Week
records.speaker: Prof. Josh Pasek
records.speaker_title: Professor of Communication & Media and Political Science; Research Professor, Center for Political Studies (I.S.R.); core faculty, Michigan Institute for Data Science
records.description: The November 3rd, 2026, U.S. midterm elections at once serve as a test of American democracy, a referendum on the Trump presidency, a decision point for the future of the country, and an opportunity to assess how the parties are jockeying for and perhaps cheating in their desire to lead the nation in very different directions. This talk will examine what we know so far about what happened in 2026 and what those results are likely to portend.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Josh Pasek is Professor of Communication & Media and Political Science, Research Professor at the Center for Political Studies at I.S.R., and core faculty at the Michigan Institute for Data Science at U. of M. His research explores how social media and psychological processes shape political attitudes, public opinion, and political behaviors. He also studies ways to improve the predictive accuracy of public opinion surveys. Prof. Pasek’s current research explores how political information might influence public opinion and voter decision-making and evaluates how use of online social networking sites such as Facebook and Twitter might be changing the political information environment. He is the author of two books about American elections, Words that Matter and Democracy Amid Crises. His work has been published in Public Opinion Quarterly, Political Communication, and Political Psychology, among other outlets.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Online only; printed "NOTE DATE CHANGE" — held Wednesday, November 11 (not the series' usual 2nd Tuesday), the week after the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. Sponsorship: DTE Energy.

records.title: “Every Person for Themselves?” How Artificial Intelligence (AI) Will Reshape the American Economy and Impact the Quality of Life
records.speaker: Prof. Jerry Davis
records.speaker_title: Gilbert and Ruth Whitaker Professor of Business Administration and Professor of Sociology, Ross School of Business
records.description: Every national economy has a distinct character — a mix of laws, norms, and habits that shape which kinds of businesses flourish. America’s tilt is toward markets: Outsourcing over in-house production, contractors over employees. AI will amplify these tendencies, using algorithms to set wages, negotiate contracts, and price goods. Left unguided, the result is an atomized economy where everyone fends for themselves, thus negatively impacting the quality of life. But smart public policy can change that.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Jerry Davis is the Gilbert and Ruth Whitaker Professor of Business Administration and Professor of Sociology at the University of Michigan’s Ross School of Business. He has spent his career studying the corporation as a social and economic force — how finance reshaped America, why large corporations are vanishing, and how to tame corporate power. His six books include Managed by the Markets and The Vanishing American Corporation. His current work examines how AI is transforming economic organization. Prof. Davis has received many awards for his research and teaching, including the George R. Terry Book Award for “Outstanding Contribution to the Advancement of Management Knowledge,” the Award for Teaching Excellence, Ross Business School, and Fellow in the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person (Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium) and online via Zoom. Sponsorship: Michigan Medicine-UM-Geriatrics Center. The Fall 2026 Gourdji series was planned by Bernard Banet, Ron Bogdasarian, Ron Frisch, Judy Gourdji, Frances Schultz, Katherine Woo and co-chairs Gerald Gardner and Marie Vitale.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
records.title: How to Think About Midterm Elections Like an Expert
records.speaker: Dr. Eric Gonzalez Juenke
records.speaker_title: Professor, Department of Political Science
records.description: We will introduce the midterms as a crucial U.S. election institution that provides a check on power. We will look at how these elections can alter the direction and makeup of the federal and state governments. We will discuss what polls, campaigns and other information can tell us about what will happen on Election Day. We will discuss how different voting blocs may affect the election results, both in terms of turnout and vote choice.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Eric Gonzalez Juenke is a Professor in the Department of Political Science at Michigan State University. He specializes in racial and ethnic politics, U.S. federal, state, and local elections, legislative representation, and immigration politics. His recent book The Presidency and Immigration Policy: Rhetoric and Reality examines how U.S. Presidents talk about immigration. His current research focuses on the election of racial and ethnic minority candidates to state legislative office in the United States.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
records.title: The Impact of Social Media on U.S. Elections
records.speaker: Prof. Yanna Krupnikov
records.speaker_title: Professor of Communication and Media
records.description: This presentation will focus on the role of social media – and other sources – in the way people understand campaigns and politics. In particular, the presentation will consider why people may turn to social media for information and the role of social media platforms in political expression. Ultimately, the presentation will consider what we gain and what we lose when we rely on social media for political information.
records.speaker_bio: Yanna Krupnikov is Professor of Communication and Media at the University of Michigan. Her research focuses on political communication and political expression. She is the co-author of books, Independent Politics (2016), The Other Divide (2022) and Partisan Hostility and American Democracy (2024). Her current work focuses on the role of the news in people’s everyday lives.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
records.title: Why Policymaking Success Leads to Electoral Failure
records.speaker: Matt Grossmann
records.speaker_title: Director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research and Professor of Political Science
records.description: Are policymakers rewarded in elections when they succeed in moving public policy in their ideological direction? Or do they face a thermostatic backlash, as citizens judge their policy moves as too hot or too cold? My analysis of Congressional election outcomes since 1948 adds information on Congressional policy actions to traditional election models emphasizing the surge and decline of presidential support and referendums based on presidential approval and the economy. I find that the electorate reacts against the ideological direction of policy, voting against parties that pushes policy further to the left or to the right in both midterm and presidential years. Even after accounting for policy and traditional explanations, however, there remains a large midterm penalty for the president’s party.
records.speaker_bio: Matt Grossmann is Director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research and Professor of Political Science at Michigan State University. He also serves as a Senior Fellow at the Niskanen Center and host of the Science of Politics podcast. He is an author of The Not-So-Special Interests, Artists of the Possible, Asymmetric Politics (with David Hopkins), Red State Blues, How Social Science Got Better, and Polarized by Degrees (also with David). He is co-owner of Hooked (a bookstore/cafe). His forthcoming book is Policymaking for Realists.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online. Sponsorship: United Health Care.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
records.title: Presidential Power and Democratic Resilience: Institutional Change and the 2026 Midterms
records.speaker: Dr. Mitchel A. Sollenberger
records.speaker_title: Professor of Political Science
records.description: Dr. Sollenberger examines how the expansion of presidential power is shaping American politics in ways that are increasingly visible in the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections. Focusing on key governing norms, he looks at how changes in government institutions, law enforcement, media, and election rules affect what citizens see, believe, and ultimately how they vote. The lecture considers what these developments mean for the role of midterm elections as a check on presidential power in contemporary American democracy.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Mitchel A. Sollenberger is a Professor of political science at the University of Michigan–Dearborn and a former analyst at the Congressional Research Service. His research centers on presidential power, constitutional law, and executive authority. He is the author or coauthor of several books, including The President Shall Nominate, Executive Privilege, and The Unitary Executive Theory, as well as numerous scholarly articles examining the modern presidency and separation of powers.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
records.title: The 2026 Midterms: What the Data Tells Us
records.speaker: Professor David Dulio
records.speaker_title: Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Director of the Center for Civic Engagement
records.description: Dulio will examine the most recent data about what to expect in the 2026 election cycle. He will also examine the major races in Michigan including the U.S. Senate contest and the race for governor.
records.speaker_bio: Professor David Dulio is a Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Director of the Center for Civic Engagement at Oakland University. He teaches courses on campaigns and elections, Congress, political parties, and interest groups. Dulio has published sixteen books, with two of his most recent being Congress and Religion: The Intersection of Faith and Politics and Campaigns and Elections American Style: The Changing Landscape of Political Campaigns, and has written extensively on U.S. elections, campaign finance, and political consultants. He also served as an APSA Congressional Fellow in the U.S. House.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
records.title: The Arctic Region in the Context of European Geopolitics and Security
records.speaker: Dr. Gabriella Gricius
records.speaker_title: Associate Professor of Strategy
records.description: Although it may seem as though the Arctic has just entered the collective consciousness with renewed American interest in Greenland, the region has long been of importance for climate scientists, military planners, and naturally individuals living in the Arctic region itself. This presentation will provide an overview of the region’s importance, stretching from Alaska, to Europe, to Russia – showing how changes in European geopolitics and security have direct implications for the future of the region.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Gabriella Gricius is an Associate Professor of Strategy at the Norwegian Military Academy and a Fellow with the North American and Arctic Defense and Security Network (NAADSN). She is also a Senior Fellow at the Arctic Institute. She is currently working on a project covering Nordic security community formation and hybrid threats in the European Arctic region.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
records.title: Four Ages of the North: The Broad Contours of Arctic History
records.speaker: Dr. John McCannon
records.speaker_title: Historian of Russia and the polar regions
records.description: Often conceived of by outsiders as primordial and timeless, the Arctic in fact moves through history like any other region on earth. This presentation will examine key themes in Arctic history—both human and environmental—tracing change and continuity over four broad time periods: indigenous, colonial, industrial, and contemporary.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. John McCannon is a historian of Russia and the polar regions. He was educated at Yale University (BA) and the University of Chicago (MA/PhD). He taught history for 30 years, most recently at the University of Saskatchewan and Southern New Hampshire University. His publications include Red Arctic (1998); A History of the Arctic (2012); and Nicholas Roerich: The Artist Who Would Be King (2022). He currently works as a guide and lecturer for Viking Cruises.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom. Bio lists only past academic posts (currently a guide and lecturer for Viking Cruises); current institution not stated.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
records.title: The North American Arctic: Myths and Realities
records.speaker: Dr. Jennifer Spence
records.speaker_title: Director, Arctic Initiative, Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs
records.description: The North American Arctic — spanning Alaska, Northern Canada, and Greenland — is often portrayed through simplified narratives: a frozen wilderness, a geopolitical battleground, or a region of untapped opportunity. The realities are far more complex. This talk explores common myths, examining how climate change, Indigenous leadership, geopolitics, science, and economic pressures are reshaping the region. Drawing on current events and policy experience, the presentation offers a more grounded understanding of a rapidly changing Arctic.
records.speaker_bio: Dr. Jennifer Spence is Director of Harvard’s Arctic Initiative at the Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs. A specialist in Arctic governance and public policy, her work focuses on sustainable development, international cooperation, and the challenges facing Northern communities. She previously served as Executive Secretary of the Arctic Council’s Sustainable Development Working Group and has held senior roles with the Government of Canada.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
records.title: Environmental Changes in the Arctic: Local and Global Impacts
records.speaker: Professor George Kling
records.speaker_title: Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
records.description: Environmental changes are occurring rapidly throughout the Arctic region, including melting sea ice and glaciers, rising temperatures, loss of snow cover and absorption of solar heat, thawing permafrost and the release of greenhouse gases, and increases in severity of wildfires, precipitation, and storms. These changes and their interactions are disrupting the function of ecosystems as well as the livelihoods and cultures of resident populations. Additionally, the changes are now having impacts outside the Arctic and are altering global weather patterns and amplifying global warming.
records.speaker_bio: Professor George Kling is a Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of Michigan. A limnologist (the study of lakes) and Arctic researcher, he primarily studies ecosystem ecology and how water, nutrients, and greenhouse gases are transferred between land, surface waters, and the atmosphere. Professor Kling is a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and has received numerous awards for his research on the impact of climate change on aquatic ecosystems from the Arctic to the tropics.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented in-person at WCC; in-person and online.

records.series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
records.title: Russian Arctic Policy, Security Strategy and International Cooperation
records.speaker: Pavel Devyatkin
records.speaker_title: Non-resident Fellow
records.institution: Quincy Institute and The Arctic Institute
records.description: What are Russia’s policy objectives in Arctic security, governance and international cooperation? How does Moscow perceive the current situation of ‘low engagement’ with the West in the Arctic, the volatility around President Trump’s rhetoric on Greenland, and the Russia-China relationship in the region?
records.speaker_bio: Pavel Devyatkin, a non-resident fellow of both the Quincy Institute in Washington, D.C. and The Arctic Institute, has published Arctic militarization, nuclear weapons and arms control, great power competition and regional cooperation. His writing has been published by the U.S. Department of Defense, Strategic Analysis, Polar Journal, Italian Institute for International Political Studies, and other outlets. He provides consultations to academic institutions, diplomats and businesses on Arctic affairs. A graduate of the London School of Economics and University College London, Pavel is an American of Russian ancestry.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom. Printed bio reads "has published Arctic militarization, ..." — an apparent missing "on", kept as printed. Followed by the ticketed Arctic Buffet Lunch (11:30 am - 1:30 pm, $20).

records.title: The Pursuit of Happiness
records.speaker: Elizabeth Anderson, Ph.D.
records.speaker_title: MacArthur Fellow, Fellow of the British Academy, and John Dewey Distinguished University Professor of Philosophy and Women’s Studies
records.description: John Locke wrote that people possess the rights of life, liberty, and property. Jefferson took that idea and changed a single word. In the Declaration of Independence, property became the pursuit of happiness, a deliberate shift meant to protect people from arbitrary domination, not guarantee personal success. Elizabeth Anderson applies that principle to the modern workplace. A boss who controls your speech, movement, and livelihood without accountability exercises the same kind of unchecked authority Jefferson opposed. Anderson isn’t putting words in his mouth; she’s carrying his argument to its logical conclusion.
records.speaker_bio: Elizabeth Anderson, Ph.D., is a MacArthur Fellow, Fellow of the British Academy, and John Dewey Distinguished University Professor of Philosophy and Women’s Studies at the University of Michigan. One of America’s leading public philosophers, she has spent four decades examining equality, democracy, workplace power, and the conditions necessary for human flourishing. Her work explores the enduring gap between America’s democratic ideals and lived reality.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person only. Anderson also gave the January 2023 Gourdji lecture on the work ethic (see Fall 2022 / Winter-Spring 2023 editions).

records.title: The Founders Warning: Did They Predict a Crisis?
records.speaker: Don Herzog, Ph.D.
records.speaker_title: Edson R. Sunderland Professor of Law and Professor of Political Science
records.description: James Madison famously observed, “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” His point was not cynicism, but a clear-eyed understanding of power, human nature, and the institutions required to preserve a republic. Two hundred and fifty years later, democratic institutions face mounting pressures that the Founders anticipated and sought to constrain. This conversation examines whether the challenges confronting American democracy today reflect the very vulnerabilities Madison warned could threaten the survival of self-government.
records.speaker_bio: Don Herzog, Ph.D., is the Edson R. Sunderland Professor of Law and Professor of Political Science at the University of Michigan. A graduate of Cornell University and Harvard University, he has spent more than four decades studying the foundations of democratic government, political authority, and constitutional order. An award-winning teacher and distinguished scholar, Herzog is the author of influential works on sovereignty, legitimacy, and republican government. His scholarship explores the enduring challenges the Founders recognized in preserving democratic self-government.
records.notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person only.

records.title: Democracy in the Age of Algorithms
records.speaker: Ben Green, Ph.D.
records.speaker_title: Assistant Professor, School of Information and Ford School of Public Policy
records.description: Ben Green’s work sits at the intersection of technology, ethics, and democratic governance. As a scholar of government algorithms, he asks a deceptively simple question: when machines make decisions that affect people’s lives — in courtrooms, in city halls, in public institutions — who is actually in control? His research examines algorithmic fairness, the limits of human oversight, and what it means to regulate artificial intelligence in a democracy.
records.speaker_bio: Ben Green, Ph.D., is an Assistant Professor in the School of Information and the Ford School of Public Policy at the University of Michigan and a Faculty Associate at Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. Trained as an applied mathematician, his research examines how algorithms and data-driven systems shape democratic institutions and public life. He is the author of The Smart Enough City, and his forthcoming MIT Press book, Algorithmic Realism, arrives this fall.
